title_original: Walter Koenig Dies: ‘Star Trek’s Original Ensign Chekov Was 90
excerpt_original: Walter Koenig, who originated the role of Ensign Pavel Chekov in the 1960s Star Trek TV series and several subsequent movies about the adventures of the USS Enterprise, has died, according to his rep. He was 90. Zachery McGinnis of Galactic Productions posted Monday on Facebook…

blocks.text: Walter Koenig , who originated the role of Ensign Pavel Chekov in the 1960s Star Trek TV series and several subsequent movies about the adventures of the USS Enterprise, has died, according to his rep. He was 90.

Zachery McGinnis of Galactic Productions posted Monday on Facebook that Koenig died of natural causes in North Hollywood but did not provide other details. George Takei, who played Sulu on the original Star Trek , also posted on Koenig’s death.

blocks.text: “Walter’s legacy extends far beyond the screen,” McGinnis wrote in part. “Through countless convention appearances and interactions with fans, he shared his kindness, wit, and appreciation with everyone fortunate enough to meet him. He understood what Star Trek meant to people and embraced the community that grew around it.” See the full post below.

Koenig played the Russian-American navigator Chekov for second and third seasons of CBS’ Star Trek series from 1967-69 and reprised the role in the first seven Star Trek films from 1979-94. The character’s introduction for Season 2 came at the height of the U.S.-USSR Cold War.

The news comes as the original hugely popular, influential and low-budget Star Trek series created by Gene Roddenberry is marking its 60th anniversary . The show also was notable for its iconoclastic diversity for a mid-century TV series.

Born on September 14, 1936, in Chicago, Koenig had a brief early career as a dancer before turning to acting. His earliest roles including guest spots on such 1960s TV series as Combat!, The Untouchables, Ben Casey, Gidget, I Spy, The Alfred Hitchcock Hour and Jericho. He also appeared in the 1963 pilot episode of what would become one of TV most popular soap operas, ABC’s General Hospital.

But his big break would come with Star Trek in 1967 — the start of a 25-year journey as the navigator of the starship USS Enterprise. The original series launched a universe that has kept tens of millions of Earthlings, known as Trekkies or Trekkers, enthralled for six decades.

“That camaraderie among Star Trek fans became more extensive when they started having conventions,” Koenig said in a2013 interview for the TV Academy Foundation. “It wasn’t only what you’d traditionally call nerds. It was people who had a sense of humanity and a sense of justice. People who had imagination and people who loved monsters. It covered a much larger canvas than was initially thought.” Watch Koenig discuss his Star Trek origins and more — including how he hadn’t watched the show before his casting — in that interview here:

Star Trek was not widely popular during its initial 1960s run, never placing within the year-end Top 30 among primetime series during its three seasons in an era dominated by rural comedies, westerns and variety shows. Its peak audience was for the pre-Koenig first season in 1966-67, when it ranked No. 52 in the three-network universe. But it began a second life in syndication during the 1970s that made it among the most popular TV series — indeed, media properties — of all time.
Koenig’s TV and film castmate Takei, who played Lt. Hikaru Sulu, paid tribute to him on Monday, writing:

“My heart is heavy. Walter Koenig, our Ensign Pavel Chekov, passed away early today. “Walter and I met on the bridge of the Enterprise in the 1960s, and we stayed friends for nearly six decades. When Brad and I married in 2008, Walter stood beside us as our best man. Just last month, on Sept. 14, he turned 90, on the same day Brad and I celebrated our 18th wedding anniversary. I will always treasure that he and I shared that date. “Walter was more than Chekov. He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man, and a loyal friend. To the fans who loved him for so many years, thank you. He loved you too. “Rest well, my dear friend. Keep navigating a steady course.

Keonig appeared in three dozen episodes of Star Trek and continued to guest on such popular TV shows as Medical Center, The Virginian, Ironside and Columbo during the 1970s, also appearing in a handful of TV movies and the 1974 feature. But his career would go intergalactic again with the 1979 release of Star Trek: The Motion Picture, which reunited the original series’ cast. Wildly popular and drenched in high-tech special effects, the film had a then-record domestic opening of nearly $12 million and ranked among the year-end Top 5.

Its success fueled five numbered sequels starring the original cast in 1982, 1984, 1986, 1989 and 1991 — all of which featured Koenig as Chekov. He also appeared in the transitional 1994 feature Star Trek Generations, which introduced Jean-Luc Picard (Patrick Stewart) as the new captain of the Enterprise, along with several other new characters who would star in more Star Trek projects.
Koenig’s death leaves Takei and William Shatner, who played Captain James T. Kirk, as the lone surviving main cast members of the original Star Trek series.

While Koenig voiced Chekov in several Trek -related video games, podcasts and other media, he also enjoyed a long screen career outside the Star Trek universe, notably recurring as Psi-Corps senior officer Alfred Bester in a dozen episodes of the syndicated space drama Babylon 5 from 1994-98.

His guest-starring TV roles during the past few decades included Diagnosis Murder, Son of a Beach, Renegades and playing himself on the animated Futurama. He also voiced multiple characters in several episodes of Netflix’s toon series Stretch Armstrong and the Flex Fighters during the late 2010s. Koenig also appeared in several movies along with numerous documentaries, talk shows, awards shows and others.
Information on survivors and a memorial service was incomplete.
Here is McGinnis’ full post on Koenigs death:

Today we mourn the passing of Walter Koenig, whose talent, warmth, and unforgettable performances left a lasting mark on generations of fans around the world. He passed of old age at home in North Hollywood last night surrounded by his daughter and niece. Best known for his iconic role as Pavel Chekov in Star Trek: The Original Series, Walter helped inspire audiences with his optimism, humor, and adventurous spirit. Beyond Star Trek, his long and distinguished career showcased his versatility as an actor and his genuine love for his craft. His remarkable talent continued to shine in his later years, most recently with his performance in the short film Mr. Fleischmann, for which he received the Platinum Award for Best Actor at the 2026 Independent Shorts Awards—a fitting recognition of a lifetime devoted to his craft. Walter’s legacy extends far beyond the screen. Through countless convention appearances and interactions with fans, he shared his kindness, wit, and appreciation with everyone fortunate enough to meet him. He understood what Star Trek meant to people and embraced the community that grew around it. On behalf of all of us, we extend our deepest condolences to Walter’s family, friends, colleagues, and the millions of fans whose lives he touched over the decades. Thank you, Walter, for the memories, the inspiration, and for boldly going where few have gone before. Rest in peace.
